content: 1. Research conducted in Botswana has explored the dynamics of pregnancy and breastfeeding in the context of HIV, with findings published in AIDS (Volume 27, Pages 1911–1920). 2. Sinha et al. (2015) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate interventions aimed at improving breastfeeding outcomes. Their findings were published in Acta Paediatrica (Volume 104, Pages 114–134). 3. Thakwalakwa et al. (2014) conducted a randomized trial in Malawi to assess the growth and HIV-free survival of HIV-exposed infants. The study compared two complementary feeding interventions alongside maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) and was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (Volume 66, Pages 181–187). 4. Thistle et al. (2011) examined the effectiveness of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV during Zimbabwe's socio-economic crisis. This study was published in Medicine, Conflict, and Survival (Volume 27, Pages 165–176). 5. Thomas et al. (2011) conducted the Kisumu Breastfeeding Study in Kenya, which evaluated the use of triple-antiretroviral prophylaxis to prevent HIV transmission through breastfeeding. The findings were published in PLoS Medicine (Volume 8, Article e1001015). 6. The 2007 guidelines by Tonwe-Gold et al. evaluated a two-tiered approach to antiretroviral treatment for preventing peripartum and postnatal HIV transmission in West Africa. This was published in PLoS Medicine (Volume 4, Article e257). 7. UNAIDS (2011) outlined a global plan to eliminate new HIV infections among children by 2015 while ensuring the survival of their mothers. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 8. UNICEF, UNAIDS, WHO, and UNFPA (2003) provided guidelines for decision-makers on HIV and infant feeding, which were also accessed online on June 13, 2016. 9. Victora et al. (2016) published a comprehensive review in The Lancet (Volume 387, Pages 475–490) on breastfeeding in the 21st century, covering its epidemiology, mechanisms, and lifelong effects. 10. Wells et al. (2009) introduced the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for assessing the quality of non-randomized studies in meta-analyses. This was included in the book Introduction to Meta-Analysis edited by Borenstein et al., published by Wiley. 11. WHO (2003) developed a global strategy on infant and young child feeding, which was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 12. WHO (2005) issued guiding principles for feeding non-breastfed children aged 6–24 months, available online as of June 13, 2016. 13. WHO (2010a) released an essential newborn care course, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 14. WHO (2010b) published guidelines on HIV and infant feeding, including principles and recommendations for infant feeding in the context of HIV. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 15. WHO (2010c) provided recommendations for antiretroviral drugs to treat pregnant women and prevent HIV infection in infants, emphasizing a public health approach. This 2010 revision was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 16. WHO (2012a) updated its framework for priority actions on HIV and infant feeding, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 17. WHO (2013) consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, emphasizing public health recommendations. This was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 18. WHO (2014) published a handbook for guideline development, available online as of June 13, 2016. 19. WHO (2015) released a guide for caring for newborns at home and in the community, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 20. WHO (2016a) provided resources on the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI), accessible online on June 13, 2016. 21. WHO (2016b) offered comprehensive information on breastfeeding, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 22. WHO (2016c) consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, with updates in progress. 23. WHO and FAO (2007) issued guidelines on the safe preparation, storage, and handling of powdered infant formula, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 24. WHO and UNICEF (2006) developed an integrated course on infant and young child feeding counseling, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 25. WHO, UNFPA, UNICEF, and the World Bank (2015) published the third edition of a guide on pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, and newborn care, accessible online on June 13, 2016. 26. WHO, UNICEF, UNAIDS, and UNFPA (2006) provided an update on HIV and infant feeding based on a technical consultation held in Geneva in October 2006. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 27. Zunza et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review on the effects of postnatal interventions for reducing vertical HIV transmission on infant growth and non-HIV infections. This was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society (Volume 16, Article 18865). 28. Chikhungu et al. reviewed HIV-free survival rates at 12–24 months in breastfed infants of HIV-positive mothers on ART. This systematic review was commissioned for the guideline review. 29. Mallampati et al. modeled the impact of maternal ART use on infant mortality, contributing to the guideline review. 30. The WHO Guideline Development Group examined the implications of updated recommendations on infant feeding guidance for mothers living with HIV, particularly in conflict or emergency settings, and the monitoring and evaluation of these recommendations.
